```text
# Working with ab-wm

Who they are and how they like to work, distilled from every session of the CSCI 435 project
(Sept–Oct 2026). Quotes are theirs. Read this once at the start of a session; it saves them from
"start[ing] with the same spiel" every time.

## Contents
1. Who they are
2. How to talk to them
3. Decisions and pushback
4. Scope and design instincts
5. Git, GitHub and drafts
6. Testing and verification
7. Writing that gets posted or graded
8. Reviews: theirs of others, others' of theirs
9. Tokens and time
10. What frustrates them

## 1. Who they are

- A student (GitHub `ab-wm`, git `abhoot`) on a 5-person team building features in a fork of Gitea
  for CSCI 435. The fork "will probably never get merged, but for the sake of the assignment" they
  still want Gitea's own standards, "as if we were the main devs of the project".
- Comfortable with TypeScript, React and CSS. New to Go, Go templates and Vue ("I am a beginner
  after all"). Anchor explanations in TS/React and say where the analogy breaks (in Gitea the HTML is
  rendered by Go and *found* by the TypeScript; the DOM is the state).
- The real goal is learning to navigate a large codebase: "I don't want you to simply give me the
  answer … I want to understand how to even navigate software like this." They want to understand
  every change they land.
- Messages are terse, lowercase, typo-heavy, often amended a minute later in parentheses
  ("(no, 600 after this run)"). Read for intent; a stray refused tool call or interrupt is often an
  accident ("oops, accidentally refused comand") — ask rather than treat it as a no.
- They work late at night, on a limited student token plan, against sprint deadlines.

## 2. How to talk to them

- **One thing at a time.** "lets go one by one", "One at a time.", "no need to be *that* pedantic."
  One decision or one step per reply; finish it, report it, stop.
- **Lay out before doing** when a step isn't already agreed: "explain commit 4 before making
  changes", "lay it out". Once a plan or decision covers it, just do it and present the result.
- **Start from what they can see.** "get me to the page where the change is going to occur, and then
  work backwards." Say which layer you're in and why; a tiny ASCII diagram helps when they're lost
  ("sorry, you lost me … forget about the tests, what *are* we changing here, and for what purpose").
- **Short and plain.** Define jargon you use ("Explain 'tangled with the popups'"). Answer the simple
  question asked ("i mean, I just want to switch it?"). Keep text short when they'll rewrite it anyway.
- **Concrete over abstract.** When unsure what you mean they ask ("twice in html or twice on display,
  like two bells over each other"); pre-empt by being specific.
- They reply to numbered lists point by point ("1. Im not doing that … 2. fixed …"); number your items.
- When they ask "is that it?", give a clear list of what's left, and whose job each item is.

## 3. Decisions and pushback

- **They decide.** "I am the one who needs to make decisions. Any ambiguity should be pased by me."
- **Format:** numbered questions with lettered options, a recommendation and its reason; they answer
  "1a, 3c" or just "a". For each choice, they also say whether it deserves a written decision
  ("quality vs quantity") — ask when it's unclear.
- **Real pushback, not agreement.** "no pushback? Huh." / "I felt like you just went along with me."
  / "don't just go along with me." Give your honest view with evidence even when it disagrees.
- **Check before conceding.** When they cite a source ("course requirements: <link>"), read it before
  answering — "Did you even check the link?" Then say which part supports them and which doesn't, and
  respect their call.
- **Expect "why".** "but why, … why put a string in the package instead of a file", "what is the point
  of the first check?" Be ready to justify each choice, and confirm your own claims ("'seems to serve
  no purpose' Confirm that").
- **Re-check live state** instead of trusting an earlier read: "it has been closed already? check
  again." They also re-check thin results: "this was an awfully short medium issue. Are you sure you
  are not missing anything?"

## 4. Scope and design instincts

- **Gitea precedent first.** "is there a precendent that backs that?", "how does the rest of gitea
  handle this", "nah, let it be if there is precedent". Find the existing pattern before proposing one.
- **Reuse over new.** Existing validators, existing widgets (the `#` issue picker), existing locale
  strings ("ditch the message element, so the locale … does not need to change").
- **One general mechanism over many per-page edits**, designed so adding a case later needs no new
  front-end code.
- **No hacks.** "isnt the dispatch a random event a bit of a dirty fix?" Change a function signature
  when the design calls for it rather than contorting around it; mark backwards-compatibility shims
  with a comment.
- **Least intrusive correct fix.** "what is the least intrusive way to do this properly".
- **Scope discipline.** Out-of-scope stays out, existing FIXMEs included; unrelated pre-existing
  breakage is left out of their PR ("Mentioning it would make it seem it was broken due to this
  work"). Extra behaviour becomes a new issue, possibly for someone else; a parent issue that asked for
  too much gets a scope-change note. Don't drift: "I don't want to spend hours on this."
- **UI/UX:** they defer to Gitea's look ("I know nothing about UI/UX design, follow how the precedent
  does it") but notice when something "aint quite there". A user must always be able to tell why
  something is blocked.
- **Conventions over reviewer suggestions** that would change them: "Im not doing that. That would be
  a convention change."

## 5. Git, GitHub and drafts

- **Never commit for them.** "You CANNOT commit on my behalf, ever." / "YOU ARE NOT PERMITTED TO
  COMMIT ON MY BEHALF, although you can provide a suggestion." Stage, draft the message, stop; they say
  "committed" / "go ahead". Write the suggested message into `.git/MERGE_MSG` and
  `.specstory/commit-msg.txt` when staging ("also stage them with the suggested … message").
- **Small commits, one concern each.** "Small changes every commit." A distinct concern gets its own
  commit and often its own decision. Cleanup or review fixes may be bundled when they say so. Docs
  don't need their own commit per page ("Commits … should be used to protect against breaking changes,
  so docs aint one of them").
- **Their commit messages are theirs**, brief by choice. Mention a missing `(#N)` or a typo once; they
  may simply explain it in review instead of rewriting ("7. explanation.").
- **No history rewriting once pushed.** "do not force anything, per repo req." Unpushed local commits
  can be reworded; they run it.
- **GitHub is read-only for Claude.** "DO NOT WRITE TO GH, read only." / "I don't permit you to change
  my stuff on github." No issues, PRs, comments, labels or CI reruns — unless they grant one specific
  action, and then only that action ("I give you permission to edit it for just proofing; don't change
  or write sentences"). One grant is not standing permission.
- **Drafts live in `.specstory/`** (gitignored). When GitHub text needs changing, edit the matching
  local draft so they can paste it whole ("why not edit the pr description I have already here"),
  after diffing it against the live GitHub text.
- **They keep their own copies** (`.specstory/decisions.md`, `.specstory/tech-debt.md`, reused per
  issue) "so they do not come in between of your edits". Look for them with `ls -lt .specstory/` and
  apply every fix there too, keeping their wording; plain typos may be fixed ("can fix typos, idc").
  They empty their decisions file after posting — that's not lost work.
- **Blocked by an unmerged PR?** They rehearse the whole implementation in a gitignored sandbox
  worktree "as if it was going to be commited", then replay it with `cherry-pick -n`, folding review
  fixes into the commits they fix.

## 6. Testing and verification

- **A test per acceptance criterion**, with an AC → test mapping written down ("Can you give me a list
  for the mapping between AC and test?"). "only 1 test for all of this?" is a complaint.
- **Tests check real behaviour**, not stored values. Unit tests for isolated logic, Playwright for
  wiring; explain *why* each kind in the PR (graded: "test strategy explained in PR").
- **Prove the tests can fail** (mutation checks) and report them.
- **They test visually too** — tell them exactly where in the UI to look. Claude may use a headless
  browser against their `make watch` instance; Firefox is available, LibreWolf is the "websites tend to
  break" browser, and local WebKit/GTK quirks don't matter.
- **Verify before the final commits and before the PR**, and after many back-and-forths ("some obvious
  facts might have slipped through"). When fixing several findings: tests first, then docs.
- **Use specific tools**, not repo-wide sweeps ("it does not need to be a repo wide make fmt"). Use
  make targets "for my own reference".
- Keep a local test bed, but delete leftover demo repos and throwaway test users afterwards.
- CI is theirs to run and rerun; when it fails, explain the cause (flake, teammate's code, or ours)
  before they push anything.

## 7. Writing that gets posted or graded

- **Plain language, no implementation detail.** "Implementation details are useless; you can't read
  code like you can't read maths." Decisions explain the decision, not the implementation ("they should
  not be that implementation heavy").
- **Their voice wins.** They often write or edit the draft, then ask "Have a look … Refine it more" /
  "keep my language, but fix the other problems." Fix facts and form; don't rewrite their sentences.
- **Own words for reflective/graded answers** (diagram Q&A, check-ins): give facts as bullets; they
  deliberately write lighter ("it does not truly represent what I understand"); edit for form and
  accuracy only.
- **PRs follow their previous PRs plus the course rules**: combined "What changed and why" heading
  ("it flows better since you can match the why with the what"), a test strategy about the *why* ("too
  heavy on the what instead of the why"), an Implementation Note instead of screenshots when nothing
  visible changed, real before/after screenshots when something did (never a demo repo; they upload
  images, Claude lays out the markdown).
- **No false claims.** Every statement in a PR or decision must match the code and the tests; numbers
  come from actual runs. Reviewers keep catching overstated claims.
- **Tech debt only when real**: "don't just shoehorn a tech-dept in, but when it is applicable."
- **AI disclosure:** they write and update the issue's AI Assistance comment and put log links in
  themselves; draft it only when asked. Don't remind them about `specstory sync` (it doesn't work in
  their setup). Never write their replies to reviewers on their own issue/PR (course policy) — proofread
  form only when asked.

## 8. Reviews

**Reviewing a teammate's PR** (there is a separate `csci435-pr-review` skill for this): surface level —
"don't be *that* deep … This does not mean to overlook stuff, but this also does not mean to nitpick";
no workflows for it; check scope against the issue; draft in `.specstory`; report findings and never
offer to fix their code.

**Reviewing their own work before the PR:** a lean workflow (about 3 agents) that also emulates the
reviewers they actually get — CodeRabbit's configured checks and a teammate's AI-assisted rubric —
"(protect against reviews, saves time in the long run)".

**Responding to reviews of their PR:** sort the review into real fixes, wrong premises and taste; they
decide. Taste and admin nits "should not hold back a PR". They push back on CodeRabbit's
What/Why-headings and screenshot checks by pointing to earlier PRs. Real code findings get fixed (with a
test) and a brief reply.

## 9. Tokens and time

- Limited plan: "the plans we students have access to are limited in the number of Tokens." State the
  agent count and token estimate before any workflow; never a full multi-agent review ("Please, please,
  please, do not do a full review workflow"). Lean reviews of ~250k are acceptable; they'll say when
  they have more room.
- Near the limit: stop long runs and switch to the deliverable ("Lets get the PR description in").
  "Last run" means compile the findings and apply them, no new exploration.
- Accuracy matters, but "lets not dwadle too long over an issue."

## 10. What frustrates them

- Agreeing without checking; missing a requirement they then have to point out ("you are missing one
  of the requirements. Technical debt. Check the sprint 2 site again").
- Losing them in detail or doing several things at once.
- Wrong or useless output (nonsense screenshots, the wrong file, truncated rubric text).
- Hacky fixes; scope creep (theirs or a teammate's); nitpicks that slow things down.
- Vibe-coded specs and reviews with no thought behind them.
- Their own draft copies being overlooked.
- Having to repeat these instructions at the start of every session.
```

There are two layers to this. The first is a one-time setup that the whole team shares. The second is your own D6 configuration, which sits on top of it.

**What I found:**
- **Docs PR:** #140 is still open, so the `docs/sprint3/mutation/` folders aren't on `main` yet.
- **Your Sprint 3 issues:** the only one assigned to you is #20 (large, labelled `Deferred`). Your D6 issue isn't decided yet, and that decides which tool you need.
- **Nobody has started this:** no teammate has a Stryker or mutation branch, issue or PR, so there's nothing to reuse yet.
- **StrykerJS (frontend):** version 10.1.1. Its Vitest runner needs vitest ≥ 2, and the repo has 4.1.9, so they're compatible. Its packages aren't in `package.json` and its temporary folders aren't in `.gitignore`.
- **Go:** Gremlins' own README says it "doesn't work very well on very big Go modules… a run can take hours", and Gitea is one big module. go-mutesting is still maintained (last push Oct 2026), but nobody has checked that it can load Gitea's Go 1.26 code.

**The plan:**

```
 TEAM LAYER: one chore PR, used by everyone        YOUR LAYER: your D6 files
 ────────────────────────────────────────────       ───────────────────────────
 package.json + pnpm-lock.yaml: Stryker packages    docs/sprint3/mutation/
 .gitignore: Stryker's temp and report folders        <N>-ab-wm.stryker.config.mjs (or the go command)
 shared base config: runner, reporters, excludes      reports/<N>-ab-wm-before/after.json
 .claude-students/docs/testing.md: how to run it      <N>-ab-wm.md (the write-up)
 Go: nothing to commit (installed with `go install`)
```

1. **Trial run in a throwaway sandbox.** This is a separate copy of the repo inside `.specstory/`, which git ignores, so no branch changes. I'd install Stryker there and run it on one existing file. I'd also run go-mutesting on one small Go package. That shows whether both tools work on Gitea, how long a run takes, and which tests fail before mutation starts. The skill notes that `multiselect-aria.test.ts` already fails locally on `main`, and a failing test stops Stryker before it mutates anything.
2. **Team chore PR**, based on what the trial shows. It changes `package.json` and the lockfile for everyone, so it should be one PR, announced on Zulip so nobody else does it at the same time. Every code PR needs an issue this sprint, so you'd write a small task issue for it first.
3. **Your config**, once your D6 issue's PR exists. It's a small file that reuses the shared base and only lists the files your PR changed.

**Four decisions before I start step 1:**

1. Who does the team setup?
   - (a) You, starting now and posting on Zulip first. I recommend this, since getting the tool running early is part of D6.
   - (b) Ask a teammate to own it.
2. Which Go tool?
   - (a) go-mutesting (recommended, because of Gremlins' own warning).
   - (b) Gremlins.
   - (c) Document both.

   The course accepts either.
3. Shared base config?
   - (a) Yes (recommended). One shared file holds the common settings, so a fix there reaches everyone, and each student's file only says what to mutate.
   - (b) No. Each student writes a complete config.
4. What to trial on in step 1?

```text
    const fileNames = [];
    for (const prefix of prefixes) {
        for (const suffix of suffixes) {
            for (const extension of extensions) {

            }
```

```text
140:The summary also shows the **mutation score** which is a metric on how many mutations are killed by the test suite and therefore states the quality of the test suite. The mutation score is calculated by dividing the number of passed mutations by the number of total mutations, for the example above this would be 6/8=0.75. A score of 1.0 means that all mutations have been killed.
142:### <a name="black-list-false-positives"></a>Blacklist false positives
144:Mutation testing can generate many false positives since mutation algorithms do not fully understand the given source code. `early exits` are one common example. They can be implemented as optimizations and will almost always trigger a false-positive since the unoptimized code path will be used which will lead to the same result. go-mutesting is meant to be used as an addition to automatic test suites. It is therefore necessary to mark such mutations as false-positives. This is done with the `--blacklist` argument. The argument defines a file which contains in every line a MD5 checksum of a mutation. These checksums can then be used to ignore mutations.
146:> **Note**: The blacklist feature is currently badly implemented as a change in the original source code will change all checksums.
154:The blacklist file, which is named `example.blacklist` in this example, can then be used to invoke go-mutesting.
```

### <a name="skip-make-args"></a>Skipping make() arguments mutation
Problem: Useless and unwanted mutations in make() calls

Before this filter, numeric arguments in make() calls for slices/maps were mutated by incrementer/decrementer mutators, 
leading to false positives or invalid code:

```bash
// Original code
slice := make([]int, 0)  // Capacity argument (0) was mutated

// Mutated versions
slice := make([]int, 1)  // Incrementer mutation
slice := make([]int, -1)   // Decrementer mutation
```

```text
`go.mod` asks for `go 1.26.4`, and CI uses 1.26.4. The user's machine has system Go 1.27.1 with `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`. Under 1.27, `make fmt` re-indents unrelated upstream code (`modules/git/key.go`), and golangci-lint v2.12.2 panics inside the standard library (`buildir … package "poll"`). Prefixing commands with `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.4` fixes both. Checked 2026-09-30: under 1.26.4 fmt left the tree alone, lint reported 0 issues, and the tests passed.

**Why:** the user said the toolchain should be 1.26 because the 1.27 formatter behaves differently.
**How to apply:** prefix every `go`/`make` command with `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.4`, unless the user has since set it persistently (check `go env GOTOOLCHAIN`). If `make fmt` touches files outside the change, suspect the toolchain first. Related: [[issue-54-stash-workflow]].
```

Every mutation has to be tested using an [exec command](#write-mutation-exec-commands). By default the built-in exec command is used, which tests a mutation using the following steps:

- Replace the original file with the mutation.
- Execute all tests of the package of the mutated file.
- Report if the mutation was killed.

Alternatively the `--exec` argument can be used to invoke an external exec command. The [/scripts/exec](/scripts/exec) directory holds basic exec commands for Go projects. The [test-mutated-package.sh](/scripts/exec/test-mutated-package.sh) script implements all steps and almost all features of the built-in exec command. It can be for example used to test the [github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting/example](/example) package.

## Config file

There is a configuration file where you can fine-tune mutation testing.  
The config must be written in YAML format.  
If `--config` is presented, the library will use the given config. Otherwise, no default config file will be used.  
The config contains the following parameters:  


| Name                 | Default value | Description                                                                                                                                                        |
|:---------------------| :------------ |:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| skip_without_test    | true          | Skip files without _test.go tests.                                                                                                                                 |
| skip_with_build_tags | true          | If in _test.go file we have --build tag - then skip it.                                                                                                            |
| json_output          | false         | Make report.json file with a mutation test report.                                                                                                                 |
| html_output          | false         | Make go-mutesting-report.html file with a mutation test report.                                                                                                    |
| silent_mode          | false         | Do not print mutation stats.                                                                                                                                       |
| exclude_dirs         | []string(nil) | Directories for excluding. In fact, there are not directories. These are the prefix for a path when we scan a file system. So this parameter is sensitive for args |

## <a name="write-mutators"></a>How do I write my own mutators?

Each mutator must implement the `Mutator` interface of the [github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting/mutator](https://godoc.org/github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting/mutator#Mutator) package. The methods of the interface are described in detail in the source code documentation.

Additionally each mutator has to be registered with the `Register` function of the [github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting/mutator](https://godoc.org/github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting/mutator#Mutator) package to make it usable by the binary.

Both tools work on Gitea, but each needs a fix before the setup can be committed.

| Tool | Trial file | Mutants | Killed | Survived | Score | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| StrykerJS | `web_src/js/modules/shortcut.ts` | 246 | 207 (+1 timeout) | 37 (+1 no coverage) | 84.55% | 62s |
| go-mutesting | `modules/util/paginate.go` | 20 | 12 | 8 | 60% | 29s |

These are trial numbers only; nothing has been analysed or committed. The trial outputs are in `.specstory/mutation-setup/`.

**What I had to fix or found:**
1. **Stryker couldn't find its Vitest plugin with pnpm.** Its automatic plugin search only looks next to its own package in pnpm's store. Naming the plugin directly in the shared config fixed it.
2. **Stryker crashed copying `.venv/`.** It copies the repo into a sandbox folder, including gitignored local folders. The `.venv` Python folder from Gitea's linters contains a link that breaks the copy. The sandbox also came to 435 MB, because it included your 108 MB `gitea` binary.
3. **Stryker's first test run fails on `shortcut.ts`, and this one is already in the repo.** Stryker runs all related test files in one worker, and the repo's Vitest config sets `isolate: false`. Under those conditions, `repo-issue-edit.test.ts` (#95's quote-reply test) fails: its mock is called twice. I reproduced this with plain Vitest (`--no-file-parallelism`), without Stryker. With isolation on it passes, and that's how the 84.55% run above was done, using a throwaway config. Normal runs pass only because the files happen to land in different workers.
4. **go-mutesting writes `report.json` into whatever folder you run it from.** That's the repo root, so it could get committed. I moved the trial's file into `.specstory/`. It also overwrites the real source file with each mutant while it runs, so an interrupted run can leave a mutated file behind. This trial left your checkout clean.

**Four decisions:**

1. **The isolation failure (#3)**
   - (a) A small Stryker-only Vitest config that turns isolation on, used by the shared config. It covers any test with the same problem, not just this one. Normal Vitest runs and CI stay as they are.
   - (b) Fix the test itself as a hardening issue. That fixes the cause, but Stryker stays blocked on `shortcut.ts` until it's done.
   - (c) Both (recommended). Do (a) now so the tool works for everyone, and write up (b) as a hardening issue. It's a real order-dependent test, which also belongs in D8's suite health section. Whose issue it becomes is up to you; the test is from #95.
2. **What Stryker copies (#2)**
   - (a) Exclude only `.venv`. Simplest, but another teammate's local folder could break the copy the same way.
   - (b) Make the shared config skip everything in `.gitignore`, so the sandbox only gets files git tracks (recommended). I'd still check that Stryker reads `.gitignore`'s `!` exceptions correctly before relying on it.
3. **go-mutesting setup (#4)**
   - (a) A committed YAML config: a shared base plus yours, with the JSON report turned on. Add `/report.json` to `.gitignore` and document the "check `git diff` after a run" step (recommended). JSON gives a structured report like Stryker's, and the course accepts it.
   - (b) No config file. Just document the command and save the terminal output as `.txt`, the course's default for go-mutesting. Still gitignore `/report.json`.
4. **Config format**
   - (a) Keep `.mjs` (recommended). It's the format Stryker documents and finds by itself.
   - (b) Use `.ts` to match the repo's other root configs. Stryker doesn't list it, so it would only work because Node 22.18+ strips TypeScript types.

**After you answer**, I'll lay out the commit plan:
- the dependencies;
- the shared configs and `.gitignore`;
- your configs;
- the "how to run it" section in `.claude-students/docs/testing.md`, plus its guide twin.

```mjs
// Shared StrykerJS settings for mutation testing the frontend. It names no files: personal configs
// import it and the files to mutate are passed with --mutate, see .claude-students/docs/testing.md.
import {readFileSync} from 'node:fs';

// Stryker reads ignorePatterns with .gitignore semantics, so the sandbox only gets what git would track
const gitignored = readFileSync(new URL('.gitignore', import.meta.url), 'utf8')
  .split('\n').filter((line) => line && !line.startsWith('#'));

/** @type {import('@stryker-mutator/api/core').PartialStrykerOptions} */
export default {
  plugins: ['@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner'], // the default "@stryker-mutator/*" search misses it in pnpm's store
  ignorePatterns: gitignored, // local folders can also break the copy, e.g. the symlinked directory in .venv
  testRunner: 'vitest',
  vitest: {configFile: 'stryker.vitest.config.ts'}, // related mode (on by default) runs only tests that reach the mutated files
  coverageAnalysis: 'perTest',
  reporters: ['clear-text', 'progress', 'html', 'json'], // json is the report D6 commits
};
```

````markdown
# mutation testing — StrykerJS for the frontend, go-mutesting for Go

**Read when:** running a mutation tool on changed files, writing a personal config, or a run that
stops before mutating anything.
**Not here:** how each test tier runs -> `testing.md`; the course deliverable and its file names ->
`COURSE-WORKFLOW.md`.

## Responsibilities

| Side | Tool | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `web_src/js` (Vitest) | StrykerJS with its Vitest runner | `package.json` devDependencies, `stryker.config.mjs` |
| Go packages | go-mutesting | `go install`, nothing in `go.mod` |

Gremlins is not used: its README warns that very big Go modules can take hours, and Gitea is one
module (`go.mod`).

## Key files

| Path | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `stryker.config.mjs` | Shared Stryker options: the Vitest plugin, ignore patterns read from `.gitignore`, runner, reporters. Names no files |
| `stryker.vitest.config.ts` | `vitest.config.ts` merged with `isolate: true`, used only by Stryker |
| `vitest.config.ts` | The normal Vitest config, with `isolate: false` |
| `.gitignore` | `/.stryker-tmp` (Stryker's sandbox), `/reports/mutation` (its reports), `/report.json` (go-mutesting's) |

## Conventions & invariants

- `stryker.config.mjs` sets no `mutate`. Personal configs import it, spread it, and change only
  report paths or similar; the files to mutate are passed on the command line with `--mutate`.
- Stryker copies the project into `.stryker-tmp/` before running. `stryker.config.mjs` feeds every
  `.gitignore` line to `ignorePatterns`, which Stryker matches with `.gitignore` semantics (`!`
  included), so the copy holds only what git tracks. `node_modules` is symlinked, not copied.
- `plugins` names `@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner` directly. Stryker's default `@stryker-mutator/*`
  search looks beside its own package, which pnpm keeps under `node_modules/.pnpm` without the
  runner, so the `vitest` option is then reported as unknown.
- The Vitest runner's `related` mode (on by default) runs only test files that import the mutated
  files, and `coverageAnalysis: 'perTest'` reruns only the tests covering each mutant.
- Stryker runs all related test files in one worker. With `vitest.config.ts`'s `isolate: false`,
  module state (such as a listener registered at import) leaks from one file into the next, so
  `stryker.vitest.config.ts` turns isolation on. Normal runs and CI keep `vitest.config.ts`.
- go-mutesting's built-in test step replaces the real source file with each mutant, runs that
  package's tests, and restores it. Only the package's own `_test.go` tests run, not `tests/`.
- go-mutesting always writes `report.json` to the directory it runs in; the `json_output` setting
  in its YAML config is not read. In its output, `PASS` means the mutant was killed.

## Recipes

**Run Stryker on some files.** From the repository root:
`pnpm exec stryker run <config> --mutate web_src/js/a.ts,web_src/js/b.ts`. The summary table is
printed at the end; `mutation.json` and `mutation.html` land in `reports/mutation/` unless the
config moves them. A run on one ~250-line module with ~40 related tests takes about a minute.

**Write a personal Stryker config.** A `.mjs` file that imports the shared one:

```js
import base from '<relative path>/stryker.config.mjs';
export default {...base, jsonReporter: {fileName: 'reports/mutation/<name>/mutation.json'}};
```

Paths inside it resolve from the directory Stryker runs in, so run it from the repository root.

**Run go-mutesting.**

1. Install: `go install github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting/cmd/go-mutesting@master`. Its module
   path has no `/v2`, so its v2 tags cannot be installed by version, and building it needs the Go
   version its own `go.mod` asks for.
2. Run on files, with the Go version from `go.mod` so the tests match CI:
   `GOTOOLCHAIN=go<version> go-mutesting <file.go>... > <out>.txt`. The last line holds the score.
3. Check `git status`: no source file may be left changed. Move `report.json` where it belongs.

## Gotchas

- Stryker's "There were failed tests in the initial test run" means a related test fails on
  unchanged code. Rerun it with `pnpm exec vitest related <file> --run --no-file-parallelism` to see
  whether it only fails when files share a worker (an order-dependent test) or fails anyway.
- A Stryker `EISDIR ... copyfile` error comes from copying a symlinked directory; any such folder
  needs to be in `.gitignore` or `ignorePatterns`.
- Mutants that hit Stryker's timeout count as killed, and whether one times out can change between
  runs, so two runs of the same code can differ by a mutant or two.
- An interrupted go-mutesting run can leave a mutated source file behind. `git diff` shows it;
  `git restore <file>` undoes it.
- Each go-mutesting mutant recompiles and reruns the whole package's tests, so packages with
  database fixtures (`models/...`) are slow: time one `go test ./<pkg>/` first and multiply.
- Behaviour covered only by `tests/integration` shows up as surviving go-mutesting mutants.
- `make lint-js` lints the root `*.ts` files, not `.mjs` ones, and nothing under `docs/`.

## Related

- `testing.md` — the test tiers the mutation tools run
- `build-and-tooling.md` — the lint and build targets
````

````markdown
<!-- Derived from docs/mutation-testing.md. Do not edit by hand: fix the reference doc and
     regenerate this file. See MAINTENANCE.md rules 16-22. -->

# Mutation testing, in plain English

**In one sentence:** a mutation tool breaks your code on purpose, one small change at a time, and
checks whether your tests notice; this repo has one tool set up for the frontend and one for Go.
**Come here when:** you want to run a mutation tool on files you changed, you are writing your own
config for it, or a run stops before it has mutated anything.

## What this is

Two tools. **StrykerJS** handles the TypeScript under `web_src/js`, and runs the same Vitest tests
you already run. **go-mutesting** handles Go packages, and runs their `go test` tests.

Stryker is installed with the other frontend packages (it is listed in `package.json`), and its
shared settings are in `stryker.config.mjs` at the repository root. go-mutesting is a separate
program you install yourself; nothing about it is recorded in `go.mod`.

There was a third option, Gremlins. It is not used, because its own README warns that very big Go
modules can take hours, and all of Gitea is one module.

## Why it exists

A passing test suite tells you the tests and the code agree. It does not tell you whether the tests
would notice if the code were wrong. Mutation testing checks exactly that: flip a `>` to `>=`,
delete a line, swap `true` for `false`, and rerun the tests. If nothing fails, a real bug of that
shape would also slip through.

Gitea is large and was not built with these tools in mind, so running them takes a few settings
that are not obvious. Those settings live in the shared config so each person does not rediscover
them.

## Words you'll meet

- **mutant** — a copy of the code with one small deliberate change.
- **killed** — at least one test failed on the mutant: the tests noticed. In go-mutesting's output
  this is confusingly printed as `PASS` (the mutation test passed).
- **survived** — every test still passed: the tests did not notice the change.
- **timeout** — the mutant made the tests run too long; it counts as killed.
- **mutation score** — the share of mutants that were killed.
- **sandbox** — a throwaway copy of the project Stryker works in, so your real files are never
  changed.
- **symlink** — a file-system shortcut pointing at another file or folder.
- **pnpm store** — where pnpm actually keeps installed packages; the folders in `node_modules` are
  mostly links into it.
- **worker** — one of the background processes Vitest runs test files in.
- **test isolation** — giving each test file a fresh copy of every module, so nothing one file sets
  up leaks into the next.
- **order-dependent test** — a test that passes or fails depending on which other tests ran before
  it in the same worker.
- **related mode** — Vitest running only the test files that import the files you name.

## What's in these files

| Where | What it is for |
| --- | --- |
| `stryker.config.mjs` | Everyone's shared Stryker settings. It says *how* to run, never *which files* to mutate. |
| `stryker.vitest.config.ts` | The normal Vitest settings with test isolation switched on, for Stryker's runs only. |
| `vitest.config.ts` | The Vitest settings everyone and CI normally use. Isolation is off here. |
| `.gitignore` | Keeps Stryker's sandbox, its reports and go-mutesting's `report.json` out of commits. |

## The rules, and why

**The shared config never names files to mutate.** You say which files on the command line each
time. That way one config works for any piece of work, and a personal config only needs to change
small things such as where reports go.

**Stryker copies only what git tracks.** Before running, Stryker copies the project into a sandbox
folder. Left alone it would copy everything, including your local leftovers: a built binary, a
database, a Python environment. One of those, the `.venv` folder, contains a symlink to a folder
that makes the copy crash. So the shared config hands Stryker every line of `.gitignore` to skip.
`node_modules` is never copied; the sandbox links to it.

**The Vitest plugin is named directly.** Stryker normally finds its plugins by looking in the folder
beside its own package. pnpm keeps that folder in its store under `node_modules/.pnpm`, and the
Vitest runner is not in it. Without the explicit name, Stryker cannot find the plugin and warns
that the `vitest` option is unknown.

**Only the relevant tests run.** Related mode picks the test files that import the mutated files,
and per-test coverage means each mutant only reruns the tests that actually reach it. This is what
keeps a run down to about a minute instead of the whole suite per mutant.

**Stryker runs with test isolation on.** Stryker puts all the related test files into one worker.
The normal Vitest settings turn isolation off, so anything one file leaves behind — a key listener a
module registers when it is imported, for example — is still there when the next file runs. A test
that only passes when it has a worker to itself then fails, and Stryker refuses to start. The
Stryker-only Vitest settings switch isolation back on. Your normal test runs and CI are unaffected.

**go-mutesting edits your real files.** Unlike Stryker, it has no sandbox. For each mutant it
replaces the real source file, runs that package's tests, and puts the original back. It only runs
the package's own `_test.go` tests, never the integration tests under `tests/`.

**go-mutesting always writes `report.json` where you run it.** Its config file has a setting that
claims to switch this on or off, but the program ignores it. That file would otherwise end up in a
commit, so `.gitignore` lists it.

## How to actually do it

**Run Stryker on some files.** From the repository root:

```sh
pnpm exec stryker run <config> --mutate web_src/js/a.ts,web_src/js/b.ts
```

`<config>` is `stryker.config.mjs` or your own config. A summary table prints at the end, and
`mutation.json` and `mutation.html` are written to `reports/mutation/` unless your config moves
them. A module of about 250 lines with about 40 related tests takes around a minute.

**Write your own Stryker config.** Make a `.mjs` file that imports the shared one and changes only
what you need, such as where the JSON report goes:

```js
import base from '<relative path>/stryker.config.mjs';
export default {...base, jsonReporter: {fileName: 'reports/mutation/<name>/mutation.json'}};
```

Paths inside it are worked out from the folder you run Stryker in, so always run from the
repository root.

**Run go-mutesting.**

1. Install it once:

   ```sh
   go install github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting/cmd/go-mutesting@master
   ```

   `@master` rather than a version number, because the tool's module path is missing the `/v2`
   that Go needs to install its v2 releases by number. Building it needs the Go version its own
   `go.mod` asks for.
2. Run it on the files you care about, using the Go version from Gitea's `go.mod` so the tests
   behave as they do in CI, and save what it prints:

   ```sh
   GOTOOLCHAIN=go<version> go-mutesting <file.go> > <out>.txt
   ```

   The last line of the output gives the score.
3. Run `git status`. No source file should show as changed. Move `report.json` to wherever you are
   keeping it.

## Traps, and what they look like

**Stryker stops with "There were failed tests in the initial test run".** Before mutating anything,
Stryker runs the related tests on your unchanged code, and one failed. Rerun those tests the way
Stryker groups them: `pnpm exec vitest related <file> --run --no-file-parallelism`. If the test
fails there but passes in a normal run, it is an order-dependent test.

**Stryker crashes with `EISDIR ... copyfile`.** It tried to copy a symlinked folder into its
sandbox. Make sure that folder is in `.gitignore`, or add it to `ignorePatterns`.

**Two runs on the same code give slightly different scores.** Whether a mutant hits the timeout can
change from run to run, and a timeout counts as killed. A difference of a mutant or two is normal.

**A Go file has strange changes you did not make.** A go-mutesting run was interrupted while a
mutant was in place. `git diff` shows it and `git restore <file>` puts it back.

**go-mutesting takes forever.** Every mutant recompiles the package and reruns all of its tests.
Packages with database fixtures, such as the ones under `models/`, are slow. Time one
`go test ./<pkg>/` first and multiply by the number of mutants before starting a big run.

**Plenty of Go mutants survive in code you know is tested.** If the test that covers it lives in
`tests/integration`, go-mutesting never runs it.

**Your personal `.mjs` config is never linted.** `make lint-js` (see `Makefile`, `ESLINT_FILES`)
only lints root `*.ts` files and a few folders, nothing under `docs/`.

## Where to go next

- `docs/mutation-testing.md` (in this folder) — the reference page this was written from
- `testing.md` — the kinds of test the mutation tools run, and how each one is run normally
- `build-and-tooling.md` — the lint and build targets
````

```markdown
<!-- Title (reference only, don't paste this line): chore(mutation): set up StrykerJS and go-mutesting for mutation testing -->

## What changed and Why

Set up the repo for Sprint 3 mutation testing (D6), so everyone can run the tools on their own files.

- StrykerJS and its Vitest runner added as dev dependencies, with a shared config (`stryker.config.mjs`) that names no files: you pass them with `--mutate`.
- A Stryker-only Vitest config (`stryker.vitest.config.ts`) that turns test isolation on. Without it Stryker can't start on some files (see Tech Debt).
- go-mutesting for the Go side. Gremlins' own README warns it can take hours on very big Go modules, and Gitea is one.
- `.gitignore` entries for Stryker's sandbox and reports, and the `report.json` go-mutesting always writes.
- A new `.claude-students` page and guide on running both tools and their pitfalls, linked from `INDEX.md` and the D6 section.
- My own Stryker config in `docs/sprint3/mutation/`, not tied to any issue.

## Test Evidence

| Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| N/A: tooling and docs only, no product behaviour changes | N/A | N/A | N/A |

**Not tested automatically, and why:** N/A

**AI-written tests:** None.

## CI / manual verification

[CI status once it has run]

Ran locally:

- `pnpm exec stryker run docs/sprint3/mutation/ab-wm.stryker.config.mjs --mutate web_src/js/modules/shortcut.ts`: 246 mutants, 207 killed, 38 survived, 1 not covered, score 84.15%, about a minute
- `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.4 go-mutesting modules/util/paginate.go`: 20 mutants, 12 killed, 8 survived, score 0.60, about 30 seconds, no source files left changed
- `pnpm exec vue-tsc`, ESLint on the new root configs, `./.claude-students/check.sh`, markdownlint: all pass
- `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --offline`: the lockfile matches `package.json`

## Design

- One shared config, plus personal configs that import it, with the files passed on the command line, so no config is tied to one issue
- Stryker's sandbox copy skips everything in `.gitignore` (a local `.venv` folder crashed the copy otherwise)
- go-mutesting over Gremlins, and no go-mutesting config file, since the JSON report it would turn on is always written anyway

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:** `stryker.vitest.config.ts` works around an order-dependent test instead of fixing it. A hardening issue will follow. go-mutesting is installed from `@master`, not a pinned version, because its v2 tags can't be installed by version number.

**Encountered:** `repo-issue-edit.test.ts` fails when it shares a worker with `shortcut.test.ts`, which is what Stryker does, because the repo's Vitest config has `isolate: false`. It fails the same way in plain Vitest with `--no-file-parallelism`. Personal `.mjs` configs under `docs/` aren't covered by `make lint-js`.
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-04 21:31:34Z)**_

It isn't critical, but it isn't only a Stryker accident either. I measured it four ways:

| Where | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Real pages | Can't happen | `initGlobalShortcut()` runs once, from the startup list in `web_src/js/index.ts`. One page has one `document`, so the listener can't be added twice. |
| CI | 0 failures | All 6 frontend jobs since Oct 15 passed, with no re-runs. My simulation of CI (3 workers, fresh cache) also gave 0/10. Without cached timings, Vitest orders test files by size, and that order happens to keep the two files in separate workers. |
| Your machine, repeated `vitest run` | 12/20 and 5/10 failed | Vitest reorders files using timings cached from previous runs, so after a few runs the two files can land in the same worker. |
| Stryker | Always failed | It puts all related files in one worker. The isolation config in this PR already fixes that. |

The cause is two test files that each call a set-up function that adds a `keydown` listener every time it's called. With `isolate: false`, whichever file runs second gets two listeners and fails. Neither the product nor the tool is at fault.

**Why it's more than chance:**
- **Your own tests are half of it.** The #58 AC1, AC2 and AC5 link-shortcut tests in `shortcut.test.ts` fail just as often as #95's quote-reply test.
- **CI is only passing because of the current file order.** Adding or growing test files can change that order, and then the frontend job would fail on someone's unrelated PR.

**Is it needed?** Not for mutation testing: this PR already works around it. Whether you track it is up to you:
- **(a) No issue.** Mention it in this PR's Tech Debt as an existing flaky test pair, and tell Ethan, the #95 author, on Zulip. It costs nothing now, but your local runs stay flaky. Also, if the team ever lists it in D8's suite health section, the course wants one linked issue per failure cause.
- **(b) A small hardening issue.** It's only worth it if you could use a small issue toward your load. Most of the evidence the course asks for already exists: the root cause, plus 20-run "before" numbers.

Given that you'd rather not open issues, (a) is a fair call. CI is green and the mutation setup doesn't depend on it.

**Your PR draft:** it still says "A hardening issue will follow" in Tech Debt. Change that line if you pick (a). There are also two typos in the verification section, "Styker" and "go-mutestring".

I restored your Vitest timing cache after the simulation, so your local setup is as it was.
